vignette:
Theresa, a 37-year-old African man, sits in the same spot on my couch each session-the edge of the cushion, back straight, hands pressed flat against his thighs. He is a psychologist himself, and he tells me he chose this profession because he wanted to understand people, to help them carry their invisible weights. He runs a small private practice in a city far from the village where he grew up. He speaks carefully, his voice low and steady, as if he is still the one in charge of the listening.

He describes the evening two years ago. He had been at a conference in a neighboring country, presenting on trauma-informed care. After the final day's dinner, he walked back to his hotel alone. The air was warm and damp. He remembers the sound of his own footsteps echoing in an empty parking lot. A man he had exchanged pleasantries with earlier in the day-a colleague, or so he thought-caught up to him. He offered to walk together. Theresa trusted him. They were both professionals.

That trust broke in a hotel room that smelled of bleach and stale cigarettes. He was pushed onto the bed, held down, told to be quiet. He says he did not fight. He froze. His body went limp, as if he had left it behind and was watching from the ceiling. He remembers the weight, the grunting, the sharp pain, and then the door closing. Alone again. He lay there for hours, naked and still, until the dawn light crept under the curtain.

That morning, he did not call the police. He did not tell anyone. He showered until the hot water ran cold, then caught a flight home. He told himself it was not rape. He was a man. He was strong. He had not fought back. He had given a presentation that same afternoon about resilience, and no one noticed a thing.

He stopped going to the gym. He stopped seeing friends. He rearranged his office furniture so his chair faced the door at all times. He started canceling appointments with male clients-first one, then a few, then a cascade. He told himself he was just tired. But he started having dreams where he was pinned down by invisible hands, unable to scream. In the morning he would wake drenched in sweat, heart pounding, certain someone was in his apartment.

He began drinking in the evenings. Not much, just enough to blur the edges before sleep. But the sleep never came easily. He would check the locks three times, then a fourth. He stopped cooking, started ordering takeout. He gained weight. His clothes felt tight, but he could not bring himself to care.

During sessions, he sometimes sees a male patient flinch or shift in his chair, and his own body tenses. He feels a flush of heat, a tightness in his chest. He has to focus on his breathing to stay present. Once, a client mentioned feeling unsafe in a relationship, and Theresa felt tears prick his eyes-real tears, which he quickly blinked away. He excused himself to the bathroom, ran cold water over his wrists, and stared at his own face in the mirror, unrecognizable.

He told himself he was fine until a colleague pulled him aside after a staff meeting and said, "You seem different. Distant. Are you okay?" Theresa smiled and said he was just busy. That night, he Googled his own symptoms. Hypervigilance. Avoidance. Intrusive thoughts. Emotional numbing. He found the PCL-5 and scored himself. Ninety-two. He did not believe it, so he took it again. Sixty-one. Still severe. He finally made an appointment with me.

Now, in my office, he tells me he is ashamed. He is a psychologist. He should have processed this already. He should have known the right techniques. He should not have frozen. He says the word "rape" for the first time aloud, and his voice cracks. He looks at his hands. They are shaking slightly. He cannot remember the last time they were still.
